items.name: Methylene Blue
items.benefits: Established clinical use: intravenous methylene blue treats acquired methemoglobinemia in adults and children. Separately, a small single-dose oral trial in healthy adults reported improved memory retrieval and changes in task-related brain imaging. That exploratory result does not establish sustained cognitive improvement, dementia treatment, general energy enhancement, or anti-aging benefit; the oral and intravenous evidence concern different uses.

source_statements.section: Who Methylene Blue Is For and Who Should Avoid It
source_statements.excerpt: This is the most important section on the page. Methylene blue has two hard contraindications and several caution groups that turn a low-risk supplement into a dangerous one.

source_statements.section: Who Methylene Blue Is For and Who Should Avoid It
source_statements.excerpt: Anyone with G6PD deficiency. Methylene blue is contraindicated here. It needs G6PD to work and can trigger paradoxical methemoglobinemia and hemolysis (red blood cell destruction). About 2% of the US population has G6PD deficiency, often undiagnosed.

source_statements.section: Who Methylene Blue Is For and Who Should Avoid It
source_statements.excerpt: Pregnancy. Methylene blue may cause fetal harm; injection during pregnancy has been linked to neonatal intestinal atresia and fetal death. It is generally avoided.

source_statements.section: Who Methylene Blue Is For and Who Should Avoid It
source_statements.excerpt: For non-emergency systemic use, the FDA recommends stopping most serotonergic drugs for at least two weeks beforehand. Do not stop any prescribed medication on your own — this requires a clinician.
Even used alone, methylene blue has predictable effects. The most universal one is harmless but dramatic: it temporarily turns urine, and sometimes the tongue and stool, blue-green.
Mild stimulation or trouble sleeping if taken late in the day.
